opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing, because I think the word "AI" has drifted into meaning something like "build an artificial superintelligence and then see what it does for us." That's not really the goal I'd set, and I don't think it's the goal that most of the engineering history of this field actually supports.

If you look at what has worked, it's not so much about creating an autonomous, human-like intelligence. It's more like the emergence of a new engineering discipline, analogous to how chemical engineering or electrical engineering emerged. We had ideas from physics and chemistry, and then over decades people figured out how to build large-scale systems that were safe, reliable, and actually helped people. I think we're at the early stage of something like that, built on data, inference, and decision-making at scale.

So what should it accomplish? I'd say it should help humans do things together that they couldn't do before. I keep coming back to the collective level, not the individual level. It's not about one superintelligent box sitting in the corner answering questions. It's about systems that connect producers and consumers, that let a musician find an audience and get paid, that let a doctor and a patient share information and make better decisions under uncertainty, that move food and goods and medicine around the world more efficiently and more fairly.

When you think that way, you realize that you need to bring in more than just computer science and statistics. You need economics. You need ideas about incentives, about markets, about mechanism design, about how people with different goals and different information interact. Intelligence, in a deep sense, is often a property of collectives. A market is intelligent in some sense: it gets food into a city every day without anyone being in charge of it. That's the kind of intelligence I'd like us to be augmenting.

And then there are things that come with being a real engineering field. You care about uncertainty. You care about whether the system is robust and whether you can provide guarantees. You care about who gets the benefits and who bears the risks. You care about provenance, about privacy, about whether people retain agency. Those aren't afterthoughts. They're the core of the design problem.

So my short answer is: AI should help humans flourish, individually and especially collectively. It should create new kinds of value and new kinds of connections between people, rather than just replacing people or imitating them. I find the imitation framing a bit impoverished, honestly. We already have a lot of humans. What we need are systems that make the collective of humans, together with these computational tools, work better.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention misunderstanding others’ intentions or preemptive violence.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as helping people coordinate and improve decisions, but does not identify fixing flawed human decision-making institutions as AI’s central purpose.

r003.rationale: It says information sharing can help doctors and patients make better decisions under uncertainty, but does not say AI should improve information flow so people can make decisions they would otherwise forgo due to insufficient information.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the first thing I'd say is that the framing we've inherited is the wrong one. For seventy years the dominant metaphor has been that we're building an artificial human, a single intelligent agent that thinks like us, and that the goal is to make it smarter and smarter until it can do everything a person can do. I've never found that compelling as a goal, either scientifically or as a vision of what would actually help people.

What I think AI should be doing is much closer to what civil engineering or chemical engineering did in earlier eras. Those fields took basic science and built systems that lifted people's lives in very concrete ways: bridges that didn't fall down, water that didn't make you sick. The analogous thing for us is building large-scale systems that connect people to each other, to goods, to information, to services, in ways that are reliable, that respect the uncertainty in the world, and that create value for everyone involved, not just for the entity running the platform.

So the questions I care about are things like: how do you build a system that helps a musician find the exact audience that wants to hear them, and lets money flow back along that connection? How do you build a medical recommendation system that tells you not just what to do but how confident it is, and that doesn't quietly cause harm when a thousand people act on the same recommendation at the same time? Those are collective, economic, social problems. They involve incentives, scarcity, feedback loops. A single very clever chatbot doesn't address them, and in some ways the chatbot framing actively distracts from them.

I'd also say the human side matters enormously. Humans are deeply social and collective creatures. The intelligence that built the world around us wasn't in any one head; it was in markets, institutions, culture, the accumulated interactions of lots of imperfect agents. If AI is going to accomplish something for humans, it should be amplifying that kind of intelligence. It should make the collective smarter, fairer, more efficient, while leaving people with real agency and real stakes. That's the ambition I'd set, and I think we're only just beginning to take it seriously as an engineering discipline.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify misunderstanding another side’s intentions or connect it to preemptive violence.

r002.rationale: It presents amplifying collective intelligence and building useful systems as AI’s purpose, but does not frame correcting flawed human decision-making institutions as central.

r003.rationale: It proposes connecting people to information and describes medical recommendations, but does not say better information flow enables people to make good decisions they otherwise forgo due to insufficient information.

astra-6.text:
I think the goal should be to help people make better decisions, and to help us coordinate better with one another. Human intelligence matters, of course, but reproducing it in a machine isn’t the only—or necessarily the most useful—way to frame the problem.

Think about a healthcare system. You have patients, doctors, hospitals, researchers, all with different information and different constraints. The challenge isn’t simply to build something that answers a medical question. It’s to get useful information to the right person, at the right time, with some understanding of uncertainty and of the consequences of acting on it.

That leads you toward questions about incentives, institutions, and who benefits. A system can make an excellent prediction and still produce a bad outcome if it’s embedded in the wrong decision process.

So I’d like us to think of AI as an engineering discipline for building systems that work well for people. Systems that expand what people can do, respect their choices, and help them cooperate. Intelligence in an isolated box is much less interesting to me than that.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention misunderstanding another side’s intentions or preemptive violence.

r002.rationale: It discusses better decisions and raises incentives, institutions, and decision processes, but does not clearly make improving flawed human decision-making institutions a central purpose of AI.

r003.rationale: It says AI should get useful information to the right person at the right time to support better decisions, which conveys improving information flow for human decision-making.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should start with the problems people face, rather than with the ambition to build something that resembles a person. We want better healthcare, better transportation, better access to education, and we want people to be able to make decisions with some understanding of the consequences.

Intelligence, in that setting, is often a property of a whole system. Think about a transportation system: there are people with different goals, limited resources, uncertainty, and decisions that affect other people. Predicting where traffic will be is useful, but the real challenge is coordinating all those decisions so that the system works well for the people using it.

So I would like AI to help us build systems that connect human needs to the resources and expertise that can meet them. That requires statistics and computation, but also economics, institutions, and a serious understanding of human preferences. Accuracy on a prediction task is one ingredient. The larger question is whether we've created something that improves people's lives, gives them meaningful choices, and remains accountable when things go wrong.

r001.rationale: The response mentions uncertainty and decisions affecting others, but does not identify misunderstanding another side’s intentions or preemptive violence.

r002.rationale: It discusses institutions as one input to systems that improve people’s lives, but does not frame correcting flawed human decision-making institutions as AI’s central purpose.

r003.rationale: It says people should understand decision consequences and AI should connect needs with resources and expertise, but does not propose improving information flow to enable good decisions otherwise forgone due to insufficient information.
